# Polished Version

In September 1607, the village of Fianaise Bhréagach was struck by an unidentified disease that claimed the lives of every inhabitant. The settlement was subsequently razed, and all official records of its existence were expunged. In 2007, an account written by the local undertaker was discovered buried among the roots of a tree in the square of the quarantined village—a find that brought the details of this long-forgotten catastrophe to light. The undertaker's testimony, rendered in verse, reads as follows:

---

*They sent a horse along the roads to say our town had been closed in,*
*its bloodied hooves had been unshod. The shoes were kept to save the iron,*
*or bless the fate of those who stayed across the glens or down the coast.*
*This horse's message came our way while sentries occupied their posts,*

*the note was tied around its neck declaring death was soon to reach*
*where all would feel its fevered knock: the butcher's shop, the mill, the church.*
*The hardest village men played tough until the store of ale ran dry;*
*the women stopped their mouths with cloth and held their husbands as they died.*

*Disease took hold with sudden force. We thought that we could hush the moans,*
*so skinned and burned the flagging horse and let the fire consume its bones.*
*My children's skin turned cold and flushed. Acquainted as I was with death,*
*I saw their end and held their trust, so cut their throats and sucked their breath.*

*I dug their graves and then some more.*

---

**Note on revisions:** I restructured the introductory paragraph for clarity and formal tone, and reformatted the verse into proper stanzas with line breaks to reflect its poetic meter and rhyme scheme (which had been compressed into continuous prose in the original). All factual details, wording, and content remain unchanged. Let me know if you'd like me to adjust the tone further or address any specific stylistic elements.

In September 1607, a mysterious illness struck the village of Fianaise Bhréagach, killing every resident. Authorities subsequently demolished the settlement and erased it from official documentation. Four centuries later, in 2007, a written testimony from the village's undertaker surfaced, having been concealed within a tree's root system in the town square that had once been sealed off. This discovery revealed previously unknown details about the tragedy.

A messenger horse traveled the roadways to announce that our town had been sealed shut, its wounded hooves stripped bare of their shoes—removed either to preserve the metal or as a final blessing for those remaining scattered across the valleys and shoreline. This warning reached us as guards stood watch at their stations, a message fastened to the animal's neck warning that death approached swiftly, destined to strike every corner: the slaughterhouse, the grain mill, the sanctuary of the church.

Even our most resilient men maintained their composure only until the ale supply was exhausted. The women silenced themselves with fabric pressed to their mouths, clutching their dying husbands close. The sickness struck without warning, spreading rapidly. Believing we could silence the suffering, we slaughtered the weakening horse, stripped its hide, and burned the carcass until fire consumed even the bones.

My own children developed cold, flushed skin—I recognized the signs, being no stranger to mortality. Seeing their fate was sealed, and trusted by them completely, I ended their suffering by cutting their throats, drawing out their final breaths myself. Then I began digging graves, one after another, until there were far too many to count.

# The Silence of Fianaise Bhréagach

In September of the year 1607, the small village of Fianaise Bhréagach met an end so complete and so terrible that history itself seemed to conspire in its forgetting. An unidentified disease—its origins never determined, its symptoms never adequately recorded—swept through the settlement with merciless speed, claiming every single inhabitant. In the aftermath, whatever authorities governed the region took the extraordinary step of razing the village entirely and expunging its records from official documentation, as though the place had never existed at all. For four hundred years, Fianaise Bhréagach survived only as a whisper, a name without a story, until the truth of what happened there was accidentally unearthed.

## A Discovery in the Roots

It was not until 2007, exactly four centuries after the tragedy, that the silence surrounding Fianaise Bhréagach was finally broken. Workers or researchers investigating the old village square—now little more than an overgrown clearing—discovered a buried account tangled among the roots of an ancient tree. The document, remarkably preserved, had been written by the village's undertaker, a man whose grim profession placed him at the very center of the unfolding catastrophe. His words, though weathered by time, offered the first detailed testimony of what had truly transpired in those final desperate days of September 1607.

## The Rider of Warning

According to the undertaker's account, as the disease's grip tightened on the village, a decision was made to warn the surrounding countryside. A horse was selected as messenger—but not saddled or shod, as though prepared in haste or deliberately stripped of the trappings of normal life. Its hooves, left bare, were bloodied by the urgency of its journey across rough terrain. Bound to this suffering animal was a note, one that announced in stark terms that Fianaise Bhréagach had been placed under quarantine, and that death itself was spreading toward the village's most vital locations—its well, its chapel, its meeting hall. The message was both a warning and a confession: an admission that whatever was happening within the village walls could not be stopped, only contained.

## Descent into Desperation

Within the village, the response to the encroaching disease followed a grim trajectory common to communities facing incomprehensible suffering. At first, the villagers turned to drink and to silence, as though numbing themselves to the horror might somehow slow its progress or make it bearable. Conversation withered; laughter vanished entirely. But as the disease continued its relentless advance, claiming neighbor after neighbor, family after family, the numbness gave way to panic and desperation. In a final, futile act of defiance against forces they could not understand, the villagers turned upon the messenger horse itself—killing the animal and setting it ablaze, perhaps believing that the creature carried some remnant of the curse, or simply needing to direct their anguish at something tangible. The fire that consumed the horse became, in its own way, a symbol of the villagers' last desperate attempt to burn away their suffering.

## A Father's Final Mercy

Yet the most harrowing passage in the undertaker's account concerns not the village at large, but his own family. As the disease reached into his household and claimed his children, he was confronted with a choice no parent should ever have to face. Watching them suffer without hope of recovery, he made the agonizing decision to end their pain himself, sparing them the prolonged torment that the disease promised. Only after this act of terrible mercy did he turn to his professional duty, digging graves not just for his own children but for the mounting dead throughout the village—a undertaker burying his own family among the countless others claimed by the plague, in a village that the world would soon after try to forget had ever existed.

# The Silence of Fianaise Bhréagach

In the autumn of 1607, in a small settlement nestled in the hill country of what is now considered western Ireland, an entire community vanished within the span of three weeks. The village of Fianaise Bhréagach—its name, fittingly or perhaps ironically, translating roughly to "false testimony"—was struck by an epidemic of such swiftness and severity that local authorities, upon investigation, made the extraordinary decision to burn what remained of the settlement to the ground and strike its existence from every parish register, tax roll, and ecclesiastical record they could locate. For nearly four hundred years, Fianaise Bhréagach existed only in the vaguest of oral fragments, dismissed by most historians as folklore invented to frighten children away from a cursed patch of moorland.

That changed in the spring of 2007, when a team of archaeologists conducting a routine survey ahead of a road-widening project unearthed a sealed lead box buried beneath the foundation stones of what had once been the village chapel. Inside, wrapped in oiled cloth that had preserved it remarkably well, was a manuscript—not an official record, but a personal account written by the village's undertaker, a man identified only by the initials "T.Ó.C." in the margins of his own testimony.

## The Undertaker's Account

What makes this document so extraordinary is not merely its survival, but its form. Rather than a straightforward chronicle, the undertaker composed his testimony in a style of lamenting verse common to Irish elegiac tradition—a form typically reserved for mourning the dead, here turned inward to mourn an entire world. Scholars who have since studied the manuscript describe it as somewhere between a keening lament and a confession, written, it seems, in the full expectation that no living soul would ever read it.

The account begins innocuously enough, describing a messenger who arrived from a neighboring town carrying correspondence and supplies. Within days, the undertaker notes, "a fever took hold of the flesh, and the flesh gave way to blackness beneath the skin, and the strong men fell first, as though the sickness sought out vigor to consume it before the weak." The symptoms described—rapid onset, discoloration, and a delirium that caused victims to "speak in tongues not their own"—have led some medical historians to speculate about an unusually aggressive strain of plague, though no definitive diagnosis has been possible from the text alone.

As the disease spread, the undertaker's verses grow increasingly fragmented, mirroring the collapse of order within the village itself. He describes neighbors turning against one another, doors barred and then broken down, and a growing hysteria that the sickness was not natural but a curse laid upon the village by some unnamed transgression. In one of the account's most chilling passages, he recounts the killing of the messenger's horse—an animal presumed by the panicked villagers to be a vector of the contagion, slaughtered in the town square and left to rot as a warning, though the warning came too late for nearly everyone.

## A Father's Final Mercy

The most devastating passages of the manuscript are reserved for the undertaker's own family. As his children succumbed to the illness, he describes, in halting and fractured verse, the moment he chose to end their suffering rather than watch the disease run its full, agonizing course. The language here abandons much of the formal structure seen elsewhere in the text, breaking into something rawer—repetitive, stammering lines that scholars have compared to psalms of grief stripped of their comfort. He writes of holding his youngest "as one holds a candle against the wind," and of an act he calls both "murder and mercy in the same breath," language that has since become the subject of considerable academic debate regarding the ethics and desperation of plague-era caregiving.

By the account's final entries, the undertaker acknowledges that he is very likely the last living person in Fianaise Bhréagach, tasked with burying a village that no longer had anyone left to mourn it—including, soon, himself.

## Erasure and Rediscovery

Historical records from the period offer only oblique clues as to why authorities chose not merely to quarantine the outbreak but to obliterate all evidence that the village had ever existed. Some historians theorize that officials feared public panic or blame for a delayed response; others suggest that the manner of the deaths, particularly the acts of familial mercy killing described in the manuscript, was considered too disturbing or theologically fraught for public acknowledgment in a period when such acts could easily be construed as sin rather than compassion.

Whatever the reasoning, the razing was thorough. No maps from the following decades show Fianaise Bhréagach; no church register lists its dead. Had the undertaker not chosen, in his final days, to bury his own testimony rather than himself succumb to the same erasure, the entire episode would likely have remained permanently lost to history.

Since its discovery, the manuscript has become a singular artifact in the study of early modern epidemics—not for what it tells us clinically about the disease itself, which remains frustratingly unidentifiable, but for what it offers as an intimate, unfiltered human record of catastrophe from someone who lived, and eventually died, entirely within it. In an era when most accounts of plague and disaster come to us filtered through the detached language of official record-keeping, the lament of Fianaise Bhréagach's undertaker stands as a rare and haunting exception: testimony that was never meant to be found, preserved by a man determined that his village's suffering, even if erased from the world, would not vanish entirely from memory.

# Fianaise: Bearing Witness in September

The word "fianaise" carries deep resonance in the Irish language, translating roughly to "evidence" or "testimony." It speaks to the act of witnessing—of standing before others and recounting truth, whether that truth is personal, historical, or communal.

September often serves as a symbolic threshold. As summer fades and a new season begins, it becomes a natural time for reflection and renewal. Schools reopen, harvests are gathered, and many communities mark the month with festivals, ceremonies, or ritual observances that look both backward and forward. This liminal quality makes September a fitting backdrop for stories of testimony and evidence—stories that ask us to examine what has passed and what remains true.

In various documentary and storytelling traditions, the concept of "fianaise" has been used as a title or theme to frame narratives that focus on witness accounts—whether from survivors of historical events, elders passing down oral histories, or communities documenting their own experiences. Such works often find their premiere or focus in autumn months, aligning the seasonal shift with a narrative shift toward memory and record-keeping.

The connection between these three elements—the specific month of September, the weighted term "fianaise," and the definite article "the" which so often precedes titles and proper nouns in English—suggests a broader theme: the human need to mark time through testimony. Whether in film, literature, or oral tradition, we return again and again to moments when someone stands forward to say: *this happened, and I saw it.*

In this sense, the coming together of season and word becomes more than coincidence. It becomes an invitation to consider how we preserve truth, how we choose the moments we deem worthy of record, and how autumn—with its natural rhythm of ending and beginning—so often becomes the season in which such testimonies find their voice.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a folk-horror short piece about a cursed Irish village wiped out by plague in the 1600s, framed as a document discovered centuries later, and include a dark rhyming poem written from the perspective of the village undertaker.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Fragment from Cill Dreo

*Archivist's note: The following pages were recovered in October 1961 during drainage works on a bog road outside the deserted townland locally called Cill Dreo — "the Church of the Wren" — in the barony of ——, County ——. The document, a vellum-bound parish ledger, had been sealed inside a lead box beneath what excavators first took for a boundary stone. Carbon analysis of the ink dates composition to between 1649 and 1653. No settlement by this name appears on any surviving map after 1655. The handwriting changes twice within the text: once from a formal ecclesiastical hand to a cruder, unsteady one, and once more to verse. It is reproduced here with spelling regularised. The ledger has since been withdrawn from public handling at the request of the diocesan archive, for reasons not stated in the file.*

---

**From the parish record, begun by Fr. Aonghus Mac Raghnaill, and continued by another hand.**

*In the year of Our Lord 1649, in the month of the blackthorn's second flowering, the cattle of Cill Dreo lay down in the field of Móinín and would not rise, and when the men went to raise them they found each beast bled from a single small wound behind the ear, as though bitten by a thing no larger than a fist. We buried them in quicklime. The priest said nothing of the old ways, but Nóra Ní Chatháin left milk on the flat stone by the ringfort that night, as her mother did, and her mother's mother.*

*By Samhain the wrens had gone from the hedges entire. Not a bird to be found, though the hawthorn hung heavy with haw. An old woman of the place said this had not happened since the year the English came the first time, and that a village with no wren in it has no watchman left between itself and what walks.*

*On the eve of All Souls a child of the Brennans, six years of age and dumb from birth, spoke a full sentence in a voice that was not her own, and what she said I will not set down, though I heard it with my own ears and have not slept a full night since.*

*The sickness came with the frost. It began in the fingers, which blackened as if scorched, though there was no fire near them. Fr. Mac Raghnaill anointed the dying until his own hand blackened in turn, and then there was no priest, and no bell but the one the sexton rang himself, alone, at every burial, because he said the dead should not go into the ground unheralded, whatever else was denied them.*

*I am not the priest. I am Séamus Ó Duibhir, who dug the graves. I take up this book because there is no other hand left in Cill Dreo to take it up, and because a village should leave some account of itself, even a village God has plainly set His face against. We are eleven souls remaining of near three hundred. The Good Neighbours have not been fed in a twelvemonth and I do not think they mean to let that debt go unpaid. I have dug forty graves in the field behind the church and there is room, God help us, for forty more. I set down here the only verse I have ever made, for I have no other prayer left in me, and no one left to say the old prayers to but myself.*

---

**The Sexton's Rhyme**

*I dug the first grave deep and true,*
*with holy water and blessed yew,*
*I said the words the priest had said*
*and slept unhaunted in my bed.*

*I dug the tenth with lime and salt,*
*and told myself it was no fault*
*of mine that Death came calling round —*
*a man must eat, the wage was sound.*

*I dug the twentieth by the moon,*
*for daylight would not last so soon,*
*and heard, beyond the churchyard wall,*
*a small dry laughter, not loud at all.*

*I dug the thirtieth for the priest*
*who blessed the rest and got no least*
*small mercy for his blackened hand —*
*I laid him down in unblessed land,*
*for there was none left to bless the ground,*
*and no bell rang but my own sound.*

*Now I dig by wren-light, pale and thin,*
*for no bird sings to let life in,*
*and every spade of earth I turn*
*shows me a face I ought to learn —*
*my mother's, and my mother's kin,*
*and neighbours I was raised akin,*
*and last of all, when I am through,*
*I'll dig a grave the exact right size for two:*

*one for the body I will leave,*
*one for whatever comes to grieve*
*and finds the feast it long has sought*
*laid out in earth, and asking naught.*

*So mark me, stranger, if you find*
*this book when I am long declined —*
*don't clear the stones, don't clear the wall,*
*don't ring the bell to wake us all.*
*We are content here, deep and dumb.*
*Leave be the ground. Don't let it come.*

---

*The ledger ends there. A final entry, in the same unsteady hand, reads only: "Eleven graves left undug. I have not the strength. Whatever comes after me, come gently."*

*No further burials are recorded. Parish registers for the adjoining townlands show no transfer of the Cill Dreo congregation, living or dead, in the years following. The townland itself was declared "waste and depopulated" in a 1657 Cromwellian land survey, its acreage reassigned without comment.*

*A postscript, in a third hand, dated 1962 by the folklorist who catalogued the find: the field behind the vanished church, still locally called Gort na dTórramh — "the field of the funerals" — has never since been ploughed. Local farmers report that no bird will nest along its northern hedge, though the hedge itself is thick and old and, by every outward sign, entirely healthy.*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Alderfen Manuscript
### Being an Account of Papers Discovered in Alderfen Marsh, Norfolk, September 2007

---

**EDITOR'S NOTE**

What follows was recovered by chance during flood-defense excavation near the abandoned site of Little Wexworth, a village that appears on no map printed after 1610. The leather-bound diary was found sealed in a lead-lined box beneath what soil analysis suggests was once a church threshold. The parish of Little Wexworth exists in no surviving Norfolk records, though a single reference in the Diocese of Norwich's correspondence—dated November 1607—orders "the matter of Wexworth to be spoken of no further, in this life or the next."

The diary's final entries are reproduced here exactly as translated from period English, spelling regularized for clarity. Portions illegible or water-damaged are marked thus: [—]

---

**FROM THE DIARY OF MARGERET HALLOW, MIDWIFE**

*3rd August, 1607*

The Bellamy child was born wrong. Not deformed—I have seen deformed, and grieved for it, and moved on. This was wrong in a way I have no word for. She did not cry. She only watched me with eyes like standing water, and did not blink, not once, while I cleaned her.

Her mother wept with joy. I said nothing of what I saw.

*9th August*

Three more born this week, in the eastern cottages. All quiet. All watching.

Old Tomkin says it is a blessing, that quiet babes are easy babes. I do not think he understands. It is not that they do not cry. It is that they seem to be *listening* for something, and waiting to answer.

*15th August*

The first adult sickened today. Widow Prickett, who delivered none of these strange children, took a fever and would not speak, only hummed—the same three notes, over and over, until her throat gave out and she hummed no more with breath, but I swear I heard it still, coming from the walls of her cottage after she died.

I am afraid to write what I am afraid of.

*22nd August*

Nine dead. The vicar has sent to Norwich for help. I do not think help is coming. I think Norwich has heard already, in whatever way such things travel, and has decided the river is the border of the world now.

The infected hum before they die. The newborns have taken up humming too, all of them, in their cradles, in the same tune, though none could have taught it to them. Mothers say the sound is peaceful. I say the mothers should stop saying that.

*29th August*

We are quarantined. Men came in wide hats and long coats and stood at the crossroads with muskets and would let no one pass, in or out. They shouted instructions from a good distance and then withdrew to a camp we cannot see.

I have started writing the names of the dead in the back pages, in case no one else does.

*7th September*

Fifty-one dead. I am beginning to hum without meaning to. I catch myself at it while I sew, while I sleep-walk, while I dig. I do not know if I have the sickness or if the sickness is simply what happens to a mind that has heard too much humming.

The children who hum never sicken. It is only the ones who resist the sound who die.

I am trying to resist the sound.

*13th September*

I found Father Aldous dead in the church, and around him, in chalk, on every stone of the floor, he had written the same six words, over and over, hundreds of times:

*THE TUNE IS HOW IT COUNTS*

I do not know what it means. I know that I have started to understand the humming as words, though I could not tell you the words if you paid me in gold. I know only that they are old, older than the church, older than Wexworth, and that the ground itself seems to remember them the way a bell remembers being struck.

*20th September*

Sixty of us left, of two hundred and eleven. I am recording this because someone must. The children—all of them infected, born already knowing the tune—are the only ones now who seem at peace. They sit in a circle in the green each evening at dusk and hum together, all in time, all in tune, and the adults who are left find it comforting despite themselves.

I am afraid of how much I have started to find it comforting.

*26th September*

I can hear them building something outside the quarantine line—hammering, orders, the particular scrape of shovels finding clay. I think they mean to bury us here, whether or not we die properly first. I think they are afraid the tune will cross the river if a single one of us walks out humming it.

They may be right to be afraid.

*[date illegible]*

I am the last who can still write plainly. I am putting this book beneath the church step because stone remembers less than soil, and I want this to be *found*, not *absorbed*.

If you are reading this: do not sing the ballad they will write about us. I know one will be written—these things always become songs eventually, that is what the tune *wants*, to be carried in a shape people will repeat for pleasure, at firesides, at fairs, not knowing what they are keeping alive.

If you hear it, whatever tune it takes, in whatever century—

Do not hum along.

*[The remaining pages are blank, save the final leaf, on which the following appears in a different hand, ink long faded to rust-brown, the meter unmistakably older than the diary itself:]*

---

### THE BALLAD OF LITTLE WEXWORTH
*(As appended, hand unknown)*

In Wexworth town the babes were born
With eyes like standing rain,
They did not cry the whole night through,
They hummed a soft refrain.

*Hush now, hush now, quiet one,
The water keeps the tune,
The ground below remembers all
Beneath an August moon.*

The widow took the fever first,
Her voice went to a hum,
Three notes she sang until she died,
Three notes, and then was dumb.

*Hush now, hush now, quiet one,
The tune has come to stay,
It walked up from the marshland dark
And it will not go away.*

They built a wall of men and guns
To keep the sickness bound,
But no wall built by mortal hands
Can hold a *sound*.

*Hush now, hush now, quiet one,
Just let the humming start,
It only takes a moment's rest
To learn it by the heart.*

They salted every field they burned,
They struck the church bell blind,
They wrote the village out of books
To keep it out of mind.

*Hush now, hush now, quiet one—*
*—was that you humming, love?*
*—was that you, just now, just there?*
*—was that you?*

---

**EDITOR'S POSTSCRIPT**

The excavation team leader, Dr. Priya Nandan, noted in her site log that two members of the crew developed an unexplained and persistent low humming tic in the weeks following the diary's recovery, which they were unable to consciously identify or stop, and which they each independently described as "not unpleasant." Both have since declined further comment.

The lead-lined box, once emptied, was found to have a very faint resonance when struck—three notes, in sequence, fading slowly, as if the metal itself remembered how to sing.

The dig has been indefinitely suspended, officially due to "flood risk assessment concerns."

The site has not been reopened.

# The Silence of Ballachrann

The village of Ballachrann does not appear on modern maps. You will find no roads leading to it, no signposts bearing its name. If you ask the old-timers in the nearby towns of the Scottish Highlands, they will tell you to leave it be, that some places are better left to rot behind their curtain of mist and heather.

They called it "the Red Sleep" — a plague that came in 1603, riding in on trade ships and rat-fur, though the villagers whispered it was the land itself that had turned against them, punishing them for some forgotten sin. It began simply: a fever, a rash blooming across the chest like spilled wine. Within days, the afflicted would beg for release, their skin weeping, their minds unraveling into fever-dreams of drowning and fire.

The kirk records — what remains of them, charred and water-stained in the archives at Inverness — describe a village that sealed its own gates. No one in, no one out. They thought they could contain it, burn it out like heather-fire on the moor. Instead, they simply ensured that no one would survive to tell the tale properly.

By the time the plague had run its course, some three hundred souls had died within Ballachrann's stone walls. The last entry in the parish register, written in a hand that trembled like a dying man's pulse, reads only: *"God forgive what we have done to spare them."*

No one knows what those final words meant. Some say it referred to the mass graves dug in haste, the bodies burned rather than buried according to custom, denying them proper rites. Others whisper of darker mercies — of fathers and mothers who could not bear to watch their children suffer the plague's final, agonizing stages, and so ended it themselves, with blade or pillow or trembling hands wrapped around small throats.

The ruins still stand, they say, if you know where to look. Cottages with their roofs long collapsed, a kirk with no bell, and a well that the locals claim runs red if you draw water from it at dusk. Sheep will not graze there. Birds do not sing in that hollow. And on certain nights, when the fog rolls thick and low across the glen, they say you can hear a man singing — a broken lullaby, soft and terrible, drifting from a house that no longer exists.

---

## A Father's Mercy

*I.*

I held my daughter's hand
and felt the fever there,
a furnace in her fingers,
her breath a rasping prayer.

The sores had come at morning,
by noon she could not stand,
by evening she was screaming
for the mercy of my hand.

*II.*

I sharpened first the kitchen blade
upon the whetstone gray,
my wife had died the week before—
I buried her that day.

I could not watch my children rot
the way their mother had,
skin peeling back like autumn bark,
eyes turning wild and mad.

*III.*

The boy went first, he was the strongest,
fought against the fever's grip,
I held him like I held him
when he first learned how to walk.
I whispered that I loved him
as I pressed the pillow down,
his small hands clutched my wrist bones
till his strength began to drown.

*IV.*

The girl was three, she called me *Da*
in words half-lost to pain,
I rocked her like a lullaby
and sang the old refrain—
*Hush now, hush now, close your eyes,
the angels wait for thee,
Da will make the fever stop,
Da will set you free.*

*V.*

I do not know what god forgives
a father's bloody hands,
I do not know what heaven takes
a man who understands
that mercy wears the face of death
when suffering won't cease,
that love sometimes must break itself
to purchase one small peace.

*VI.*

I dug the graves before the dawn,
no priest to say the words,
just wind across the empty glen
and silence where their laughter stirred.
And now I wander empty rooms
where once I heard them play,
and wonder why the Red Sleep spared
the one who had to slay.

*VII.*

They'll find my body come the spring,
another soul the plague has claimed,
but know it was not fever, no—
'twas grief that knew my name.
I could not live beyond the act
of what my hands had done,
so here's my epitaph, complete:
*He loved. He lost. He's gone.*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Undertaker's Ledger

*Found in the archives of a demolished chapel, 1987. The leather binding had fused with mold; the ink, in places, had turned the color of old blood.*

---

The village of Aldermere does not appear on any map made after 1666. The Crown's surveyors, when asked, would only say that the land had been "returned to God" and change the subject. For three hundred years, the forest reclaimed what men abandoned, until a road crew clearing timber struck the corner of a stone foundation—and beneath it, wrapped in oiled canvas and buried like a sin, the ledger of a man who signed himself only as *Corwin, Keeper of the Dead.*

His early entries are mundane. Names. Dates. The price of pine coffins. But by midsummer, the handwriting changes—smaller, faster, pressing hard enough to tear the page—as the fever arrives and does not leave.

He writes of the village elders sealing the roads with felled trees, of watchtowers manned by boys with pitchforks, of the well running foul. He writes of the bishop's messenger, sent for on the ninth day, who never returned—and of the horse that came back alone, three weeks later, its coat scorched, its eyes rolled white with something that was not merely fear.

It is here that Corwin's prose breaks into verse, as if language itself could no longer hold the shape of what he witnessed:

---

*A horse came down through Widow's Pass*
*with no rider on its back,*
*its flanks were scored as if by lash,*
*its hooves left prints of black.*

*We asked it questions with our eyes—*
*the beast could only scream—*
*for it had seen what waits outside*
*and would not wake from dream.*

*We burned the dead by candle's light,*
*for burial took too long,*
*and bones don't ask you why they're right*
*to be consumed by song*

*of fire, fire, hungry fire,*
*that eats the plague and name,*
*that turns a soul to climbing pyre*
*and calls it holy flame.*

*The children pressed their palms to glass*
*that once had shown the sky,*
*and begged the road to let them pass—*
*the road said, let them die.*

*For no one came from bishop's hall,*
*no rider, priest, nor king,*
*we were a name upon a wall*
*that no one cared to sing.*

*So Corwin keeps the book of bones,*
*and Corwin lights the pyre,*
*and Corwin sits among the stones*
*and feeds the growing fire.*

---

The entries end mid-sentence on what would have been the forty-first day. The final legible words, smeared as though touched by a wet thumb—or a tear—read: *I am the last who writes. I am the last who—*

The road crew reported the foundation stones were arranged in a perfect circle, blackened at the center, though no one could explain why the burn pattern radiated *outward*, as if the fire had begun in the earth itself and reached up, hungry, toward the sky.

They filled the hole in by nightfall.

No one asked why the birds had gone silent, or why the horses hired for the excavation refused, all that week, to be led anywhere near Widow's Pass.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Hollowmere Testament

## I. What the Archive Yields

In the register of St. Bartholomew's-in-the-Fen, the parish rolls run without incident from 1611 to the spring of 1666, at which point the hand changes—grows cramped, hurried, blotted—and then simply stops. No entry follows for eleven years. When the record resumes, it is in a different hand entirely, and it opens with a single line: *"Of Hollowmere there is nothing more to say."*

The village itself no longer appears on any map made after 1670. Where it stood, three miles east of the church along the old sheep-path, there is now only a green swell of earth too regular to be natural, a stand of alder that will not burn cleanly, and a single yew, black-barked and leaning, that the local children are told never to sit beneath. The oldest families in the district say the village was "shut up"—not abandoned, *shut up*—during the plague year, and that what was done there was of a kind that no bishop would absolve and no coroner would rule upon.

In 1839, workmen repairing the crypt wall of St. Bartholomew's found a lead box mortared into the foundation, so placed that it could only have been sealed from within the wall itself, by someone who then had the wall closed behind him. Inside, wrapped in oiled cloth gone black with age, was a manuscript. It is unsigned in the ordinary sense, though the writer names himself within it. What follows is transcribed from that document, preserving as nearly as possible its original form: a testimony set down in verse, after the manner of the ballads then sung at market and fair, by a man recording, as he says, "each day its horror, that some record might outlast the hand that made it."

---

## II. The Testament of Nathaniel Grey, Clerk of Hollowmere

*Set down in the year of our Lord 1666, in the parish of Hollowmere, by my own hand, that truth might survive where I do not.*

I write this by a tallow stub
With rain upon the pane,
That God, if not my living kin,
May know we did not feign.

The first to fall was Agnes' boy,
Found blackened in his bed;
She would not credit it was true
Till she herself lay dead.

*The ninth day of July*

The reeve cried out that we should flee,
The priest cried out to pray,
The miller nailed his shutters fast
And turned all folk away.

By Lammastide we'd buried more
Than lived to dig the graves,
And still the dead came faster than
The living dug their staves.

*The second week of August*

There came a knocking in the night
At doors already shut—
Not fist, I think, nor knuckle bare,
But something dragged, and cut.

I do not write what I believe.
I write what I have seen:
That Goodwife Marsh, three days interred,
Was found where she had been.

The bell of Bartholomew's tolled
Though no man pulled the rope.
The sexton swore before he died
It rang out like a hope

Turned inside-out, a joyful sound
Grown foul within its throat—
As if some other hand had learned
The shape of a church note.

*The feast of the Assumption*

We took the sick into the church,
Some forty souls or more,
For there was room, and none to spare
In any other door.

I helped to seal them in myself.
I will not name who bid it done.
The oak was thick, the bar was iron,
We worked before the sun.

Old Marren begged us at the last,
Her boy still at her breast—
I have his voice yet in my ear.
I did not know the rest

Of what a man might carry home
And call it mercy still.
God knows I meant to save the town.
I do not know God's will.

*Michaelmas*

For three nights we heard singing there,
A girl's voice, thin and clear,
Some hymn none of us living knew,
Grown fainter each night we'd hear.

The fourth night there was silence, whole
And total, walled within,
And that was worse than any cry
That plague or death had been.

*October, the day uncertain*

My daughter took the fever Tuesday last,
My wife by Friday eve.
I dug what grave my strength allowed
And had no strength to grieve.

I am the only hand that writes
In all this parish now.
The register lies open still
Where I set down my vow

To leave some word of what befell,
Not for the Church's sake,
Nor for my own soul's easing, but
Because the dead can't speak.

*No date is given after this*

I feel the fever in my blood,
The mark begun to show.
I've sealed this in the crypt-wall stone
Where none but God will know,

Unless in some far kinder year
A hand undoes my work,
And reads what I could not confess
To priest, or bell, or kirk—

That we walled living souls to save
The lives of other men,
And I set my own hand to it,
And I would do't again,

And that is why I hide this page
Instead of burning it—
So it may judge me, or absolve,
Long after I have—

---

## III. The Wall Closed Behind Him

The manuscript ends there, mid-line, the final word unwritten or worn past legibility—the transcriber cannot say
